candidate_title: Commonsense Visual Sensemaking in Autonomous Driving: Neurosymbolic Online Abduction Integrating Vision and Semantics
candidate_abstract: This work demonstrates the need for and potential of systematically integrating vision and semantics for visual sensemaking in autonomous driving. The study develops a general neurosymbolic approach to online visual sensemaking, systematically formalizes it, and fully implements it using answer set programming (ASP). The approach incorporates state-of-the-art visual computing into a modular framework that can be used within hybrid architectures for real-time perception and control. Evaluation uses the community-established KITTIMOD, MOT-2017, and MOT-2020 benchmarks. In safety-critical driving, the work highlights human-centred visual sensemaking through semantic representation, explainability, question-answering, and commonsense interpolation. The framework is domain-independent; autonomous driving serves as an example of online visual sensemaking across diverse cognitive interaction settings, considered in relation to selected human-centred AI technology-design considerations.

Recognizing human actions in video requires representing interactions between spatial features and their temporal evolution. This work proposes novel tensor-based representations for compactly capturing these higher-order relationships. The two proposed representations are the Sequence Compatibility Kernel (SCK), which models spatio-temporal feature correlations, and the Dynamics Compatibility Kernel (DCK), which models the dynamics of an action sequence. The generalized SCK(+), operating on subsequences, captures the local-global interplay of correlations and can incorporate multimodal inputs such as 3D skeleton joints and per-frame classifier scores from deep-learning video models. Linearized versions of the kernels provide compact, fast descriptors. Experiments cover 3D skeleton action sequences, fine-grained video sequences, and standard non-fine-grained videos. The resulting tensors represent higher-order feature co-occurrences relevant to fine-grained recognition. The authors use higher-order tensors and so-called Eigenvalue Power Normalization (EPN), which have long been speculated to perform spectral detection of higher-order occurrences, thereby capturing fine-grained feature relationships rather than merely counting features in action sequences. The authors prove that coupling EPN with an order-r tensor built from Z*-dimensional features yields a Tensor Power Normalization metric endowed with binom(Z*,r) detectors, each associated with an r-dimensional subspace represented by the tensor, such that the metric detects whether at least one higher-order occurrence is ‘projected’ into that subspace.

candidate_title: SG-Net: Syntax-Guided Transformer for Language Representation
candidate_abstract: Representing language effectively requires modeling linguistic information in long, complex texts while reducing interference from irrelevant material. Standard attention mechanisms do not impose explicit constraints on which words receive attention, so they may emphasize dispensable terms. This work introduces syntactic constraints into attention to produce linguistically motivated representations. Within a Transformer-based encoder, syntactic dependency of interest (SDOI) is incorporated into a self-attention network (SAN), creating an SDOI-SAN with syntax-guided self-attention. SG-Net combines this component with the original Transformer SAN in a dual-context architecture. The approach is applied to typical Transformer encoders. The authors report extensive experiments on benchmarks for natural language inference and machine reading comprehension, as well as neural machine translation. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of SG-Net.

Machine translation of Japanese comics must address both context dependence and the combination of text with visual information. Because manga intermixes text and images in an unstructured layout, image-derived context is important for translation, yet extracting and integrating that context into translation models remains an open problem. Suitable training corpora and evaluation benchmarks were also unavailable. This work makes four contributions: a multimodal, context-aware translation framework that incorporates information from manga images; an automatic method for constructing parallel training corpora from original manga and their translations without manual labeling; a benchmark for evaluating manga translation; and a comprehensive system for fully automated manga translation. The framework enables translation of speech-bubble text that cannot be translated adequately without contextual information, such as text in other speech bubbles or information about the speaker's gender. The authors present the framework as the first to incorporate context obtained from manga images and the system as the first comprehensive system for fully automated manga translation.

candidate_title: Towards Fairness in Deep Anomaly Detection
candidate_abstract: Anomaly detection identifies unusual instances and is a fundamental data-science task. Deep methods for anomaly detection have delivered superior performance, especially on complex inputs such as images. This work studies deep one-class classification, which learns a mapping using only normal samples. Because deep networks apply nonlinear transformations, their learned representations may capture patterns associated with social bias. The central challenge is to make anomaly predictions both fair and correct. The proposed Deep Fair SVDD architecture is trained with an adversarial network to reduce the association between sensitive attributes and learned representations, rather than incorporating fairness only through a regularizer or constraint. The study proposes two effective fairness measures, and its experiments expose fairness deficiencies in previously developed deep anomaly detectors. Experiments show that the proposed method can largely remove unfairness with minimal loss in anomaly-detection performance. The analysis examines the model's strengths and limitations through parameter analysis, feature visualization, and run-time analysis.
